lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: It means remembering the result of a function call, so the same call never has to be worked out twice.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Think of a calculator with a notepad. Before calculating, check the notepad. If the answer is there, just read it.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Here is a function, [square|square|c]. It prints compute, whenever it really does the work.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The [memo|memo|c] function wraps it. It creates a cache, a [Map|map|c], that lives in a closure.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Inside, it first asks: does the cache already have this input? If {true}, return the saved answer.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Otherwise, run the real function, save the result in the cache, and return it.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Call it with nine. A cache miss. It prints compute, and returns eighty one.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Call it with nine again. A cache hit. No compute, same answer, instantly.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Now four. A new input, so a miss. Compute, sixteen.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Recursion. Fibonacci of twenty, done the plain way, calls the function twenty one thousand, eight hundred and ninety one times.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: With a cache, the same answer takes just twenty one calls.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The trade is memory for speed.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Use it only for pure functions, which always return the same output for the same input.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Exactly. A closure for the cache, and a pure function inside.
